## What prompt caching is

An LLM API is stateless. Every request sends the whole prompt again. The model must process every input token each time, and you pay for every token each time.

Prompt caching stores the processed form of the front part of your prompt on the server. A later request that repeats that same front part reads the stored form. You pay a reduced rate for those tokens. Latency drops as well, because the model skips the work.

The closest analogy from backend work is an HTTP `ETag`, with one hard difference. An `ETag` matches a whole resource. This cache matches a *prefix* only. A prefix is the run of tokens from the very start of the prompt up to some point.

## The mechanism is a prefix match

This is the whole reason order matters. The server compares your new prompt to the cached copy from token 1 forward. It stops at the first token that differs. The rule is:

1. Tokens before the first difference are a cache hit. You pay the cheap read rate.
2. Tokens from the first difference to the end are a miss. You pay the full input rate.
3. One changed token near the front destroys the cache for everything after it.

The API assembles the prompt in a fixed order, and the cache reads it in that same order:

1. `tools` — your tool definitions
2. `system` — the system prompt
3. `messages` — the conversation turns, oldest first

So a change to one tool definition invalidates the system prompt and the whole conversation, even when neither of those changed.

## Why this decides your prompt layout

Put the stable content first. Put the volatile content last. Never let a variable value sit in front of a large constant one.

Here is the failure case. Your app answers questions about a 20,000-token document.

```python
# BAD — the question changes every call, so nothing after it ever caches.
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": f"Question: {user_question}"},
    {"type": "text", "text": document},          # 20k tokens, re-billed in full every call
]}]

# GOOD — the document is a stable prefix and caches.
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": document,
     "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},    # marks the end of the cacheable prefix
    {"type": "text", "text": f"Question: {user_question}"},
]}]
```

Both prompts contain the same tokens. The first one caches nothing. The second one caches 20,000 tokens.

Two more cases follow the same rule:

- **A timestamp or a session id in the system prompt.** This changes on every call and sits at the front. It voids the cache for the entire request. Move it into the last user message.
- **A multi-turn chat.** Old turns never change, and the new turn goes on the end. The conversation caches well by its nature. Do not reorder or edit old turns.

## Breakpoints

You mark the end of a cacheable prefix with `cache_control` on a content block. You do not mark the start. The start is always token 1 of the prompt.

You get up to 4 breakpoints per request. The server checks each of them on a read, so it can fall back to an earlier breakpoint when a later section changes. A common layout uses one breakpoint after `tools`, one after `system`, and one after the last stable conversation turn.

## Costs and lifetime — verify these

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Cache write | About 1.25x the base input rate |
| Cache read | About 0.1x the base input rate |
| Default lifetime | 5 minutes |
| Optional longer lifetime | 1 hour, at a higher write rate |
| Minimum cacheable prefix | About 1024 tokens; higher on the small models |

Three consequences matter for your design:

1. A write costs more than a plain input token. A prefix that you read once is a net loss. A prefix that you read many times pays back fast.
2. Each cache hit resets the lifetime clock. A steady request flow keeps a cache warm without a rewrite.
3. A prefix shorter than the minimum does not cache at all, and the request succeeds with no error. Read the `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` fields in the response `usage` object to confirm that your cache works.
